summary: What distinguishes the faith that justifies from intellectual assent or temporary belief, knowledge, assent, and trust
readingInstruction: Read James 2:14-26 and Hebrews 11:1-6. Today is a doctrinal pause on saving faith. Notice what James says dead faith lacks and what Hebrews says living faith does.
settingTheScene: What is saving faith? The question matters for every Christian. Paul says we are justified by faith alone, apart from works of the law. James says a person is justified by works and not by faith alone. Hebrews gives a portrait of faith in action. Taken together, the New Testament teaches that faith is the only way we receive Christ, and that the faith which receives him always leads to a changed life.
observation: “I will show you my faith by my works” (James 2:18).
“You see that faith was active along with his works, and faith was completed by his works” (James 2:22).
“Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness” (James 2:23).
“Now faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen” (Hebrews 11:1).
“By faith Abel offered to God a more acceptable sacrifice than Cain” (Hebrews 11:4).
“By faith Enoch was taken up so that he should not see death” (Hebrews 11:5).
“And without faith it is impossible to please him, for whoever would draw near to God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him” (Hebrews 11:6).
doctrinalFocus:
Saving faith is the God-given trust by which a sinner rests on Christ alone for salvation. It is a gift of God (Ephesians 2:8-9) and the instrument, not the ground, by which we are justified. Our faith does not earn anything; it receives what Christ has earned.

The older theologians distinguished three elements. Knowledge (notitia): we must know the facts of the gospel, who Jesus is and what he has done. Assent (assensus): we must agree that these facts are true. Trust (fiducia): we must personally rest on Christ and entrust ourselves to him. The demons have the first two, and even tremble, but they do not have the third. Saving faith is not just believing that, but believing in: relying on a person.

Faith alone, but never alone. This phrase summarizes the Reformation teaching. We are justified by faith alone, not by faith plus works. But the faith that justifies is never by itself; it always produces works, because the Spirit who gives faith also gives new life. Works are the fruit and evidence of faith, not the root of salvation. That is why Paul can say that a person is counted righteous apart from works of the law (Romans 3:28; 4:5), and also that the only thing that counts is “faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6).

How do Paul and James fit together? Several observations help. First, they address different opponents: Paul faces legalists who rely on works of the law, and James faces people who claim faith but live in disobedience. Second, they use the word “justify” somewhat differently: for Paul, it is God’s declaration that a sinner is righteous; for James, in this context, it is the vindication of a claim to faith by the evidence of works (compare Matthew 11:19). Third, they mean different things by “faith”: for Paul, it is trusting in Christ; for James, the faith in view is a bare profession. Both use Abraham to make their point, and both quote Genesis 15:6.

Other traditions explain the relationship differently. The Roman Catholic Church teaches that justification includes an inward renewal and is advanced by cooperation with grace through works of love. Some Arminian traditions emphasize that faith must continue for salvation to continue. Evangelicals who hold to progressive covenantalism and Reformed convictions teach that justification is a once-for-all declaration received by faith alone, which is inseparable from sanctification. We should read James as correcting a dead orthodoxy, not as overturning Paul.

Hebrews 11 shows what living faith looks like. It is “the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen.” Abel, Enoch, and Noah all acted on what God said, even when they could not see the result. “Without faith it is impossible to please him.” Faith is not wishful thinking; it is confident trust in the God who speaks and promises.
interpretation:
James presents a test: can you show your faith? “I will show you my faith by my works.” He is not saying works replace faith. He is saying that invisible faith becomes visible by what it does. Think of a tree: you know what kind it is by its fruit. Faith in a good God leads to love for neighbor, in the way that trust in a doctor leads to following his prescription.

His example is Abraham, who offered Isaac. Abraham had been counted righteous in Genesis 15, many years earlier, when he simply believed God. In Genesis 22, his obedience demonstrated that his faith was real. “Faith was active along with his works, and faith was completed by his works.” Completed here means brought to its intended end, its full expression, not that something was lacking in the faith. The “fulfilled” Scripture is Genesis 15:6: what God declared about Abraham was shown to be true.

Hebrews 11 gives the same picture from another angle. Faith believes that God exists and that he rewards those who seek him. Abel offered a better sacrifice because he trusted God; Enoch walked with God and was taken; Noah built an ark. Each acted on a word from God. In every case, faith moves people to act. So the question for us is not only “Do I believe?” but “Whom do I trust, and what does my life show?”

The comfort here is that faith is not a work we produce to earn God’s favor. A small faith in a great Savior saves. The Lord can work with a mustard seed. But the faith that saves does not stay inactive.
connection: Ephesians 2:8-10 joins grace, faith, and works. Romans 3:28, 4:1-5, and Galatians 2:16 give Paul’s statements on justification by faith. Galatians 5:6 speaks of faith working through love. Genesis 15:6 and 22:1-19 are the two scenes from Abraham’s life. Matthew 7:16-20 says we know a tree by its fruit. Matthew 17:20 says faith like a mustard seed is enough. John 6:28-29 says the work of God is to believe in the one he sent. Titus 2:11-14 and 3:8 tie grace to good works. Mark 9:24 is the prayer, “I believe; help my unbelief!”
application:
Ask yourself the three questions: Do I know the gospel? Do I agree it is true? Have I put my whole trust in Christ to save me?

If you doubt your faith, look not for a perfect record but for a direction: are you growing in love for God and neighbor?

Choose one act of obedience that expresses your trust in God today.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for the gift of faith.
Tell him that you trust in Christ alone, not in your works.
Ask him to let that faith show in what you do.
